claims.text: Superconductivity in layered high-entropy alloy superconductors is primarily governed by effective in-plane chemical pressure.
Atomic-scale configurational disorder creates effective in-plane chemical pressure.
Configurational disorder alters local bond lengths.
Configurational disorder alters interlayer interactions.
Disorder-induced structural changes modify the electronic density of states.
Disorder-induced in-plane chemical pressure enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Modification of the density of states at the Fermi level enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling raises the superconducting transition temperature.
The targeted layered high-entropy superconductors possess significant configurational disorder on in-plane atomic sites.
Varying constituent elements or their ratios can systematically tune configurational entropy.
Changing constituent elements or their ratios will alter effective in-plane chemical pressure.
Atomic-scale elemental mixing induces local distributions of in-plane bond lengths and interlayer spacings.
Samples with higher effective in-plane chemical pressure will have a higher superconducting transition temperature.
Samples with higher configurational disorder will have a higher superconducting transition temperature.
Higher-disorder samples will exhibit more robust zero-resistance behavior than lower-entropy ordered samples.
Reduced configurational disorder produces a more uniform in-plane chemical environment.
The proposed mechanism is significant in layered structures because anisotropic bonding permits in-plane bond modulation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to isotropic three-dimensional high-entropy superconductors.
Impurities and defects may influence the relationship between disorder, chemical pressure, and transition temperature.

A lack of a statistically significant transition-temperature increase, or a lack of detectable bond-environment or density-of-states modification in the high-disorder samples, would falsify the hypothesis.
